programs.name: Department of Human Services Division of Aging Services (State Unit on Aging)
programs.federal_name: Older Americans Act Title III-B and Title III-E (Area Agencies on Aging)
programs.about: Georgia's aging agency funds local Area Agencies on Aging, which may pay for home safety checks and small modifications. Use the Eldercare Locator line to find your local office.

programs.name: Georgia's Assistive Technology Act Program, Tools for Life
programs.about: Georgia's assistive technology program can help people with disabilities find, try or pay for devices and home changes.

programs.name: Georgia Centers for Independent Living
programs.about: Use this directory to find a Center for Independent Living near you in Georgia; some can help with home modification.

programs.name: Specially Adapted Housing (SAH) and Special Housing Adaptation (SHA) Grants
Home Improvements and Structural Alterations (HISA) Grant
Georgia Vocational Rehabilitation Agency
programs.about: Georgia's vocational rehabilitation agency may cover home changes when they help a person with a disability work toward a job goal.

programs.name: Home and Community-Based Services Program/In-Home Services
programs.about: Georgia's aging division runs in-home services for older adults. Home repair and modification can be part of the help.

programs.name: Health, long-term care and life insurance
Georgia Medicaid
programs.federal_name: Medicaid Home and Community-Based Services (HCBS) Waivers
programs.about: Georgia Medicaid runs home and community-based waivers that may pay for home changes like ramps or grab bars for people who qualify. Rules and waiver names vary, so check with the agency.

programs.name: Georgia's Money Follows the Person Program
programs.about: Georgia's Money Follows the Person program helps people move from a nursing home back to the community. Help with home setup may be part of the plan.

programs.name: Social Security: Plan for Achieving Self-Support (PASS) and Impairment-Related Work Expenses (IRWE)
programs.about: People on SSI or SSDI may be able to set aside money for home changes tied to work or independence without losing as much in benefits.

programs.name: Local Housing/Neighborhood Agencies (Neighborhood Housing Services)
programs.about: Local nonprofit housing groups in Georgia, such as NeighborWorks members, may offer repair help, advice or low-cost loans. Search your city name plus "Neighborhood Housing Services."

programs.name: Georgia Department of Community Affairs/Georgia Housing Finance Authority
programs.about: Georgia Department of Community Affairs/Georgia Housing Finance Authority is Georgia's housing finance agency. Agencies like this may offer low-interest or deferred loans for home repairs for low- and moderate-income households.

programs.name: Section 504 Home Repair Loans and Grants
programs.about: Contact the Georgia USDA Rural Development office for 504 help in rural areas.

programs.name: Section 533 Rural Housing Preservation Grants
programs.about: USDA gives these grants to local governments, nonprofits and Tribes, which then fix up homes of low-income people in small rural towns. Ask local groups if they have this money.

programs.name: Georgia Weatherization Assistance Program
programs.about: Georgia's weatherization program makes homes of low-income households more energy efficient and can fix some safety problems along the way.

programs.name: FHA Title I Home Improvement Loan
programs.about: A federally insured loan from approved local lenders that can pay for fixing up an existing home.

programs.name: Home Equity Line of Credit
programs.about: Homeowners can borrow against their home's value as needed to pay for changes. The home backs the loan, so payments must be kept up.

programs.name: Home Equity Loan
programs.about: A second mortgage that gives a lump sum for home changes, paid back on top of the first mortgage.

programs.name: Lender Unsecured/Personal Loans
programs.about: A bank personal loan can cover smaller projects. It works for renters too, since the home is not used as security.

programs.name: Mortgage Refinancing
programs.about: Replacing your current mortgage with a new, larger one can free up cash for home changes if you have enough equity.

programs.name: Remodeler Donated Financing
programs.about: Some contractors donate labor, materials or an unsecured loan for part of a project. Ask your remodeler.

programs.name: Remodeler Referred Financing
programs.about: Many remodelers work with finance companies that offer project loans. Ask your contractor what they offer and compare costs.

programs.name: Secured Loans Against Homeowner's Bank Accounts
programs.about: You may be able to borrow against a CD or savings at your bank to pay for smaller home changes.

programs.name: Secured Loans Against Homeowner's Financial Investment Accounts (Margin Loan)
programs.about: A margin loan borrows against an investment account. It can pay for home projects, but it carries market risk.

programs.name: Civic, Advocacy, Religious, and Trade Groups
programs.about: Churches, service clubs and builder groups sometimes build ramps or raise money for home changes. Call 211 to find groups near you.

programs.name: Georgia Crime Victims Compensation Program
programs.federal_name: Crime Victims' Benefits (U.S. Department of Justice)
programs.about: Georgia's crime victim compensation program may pay for home access changes when a crime caused an injury and other sources don't cover it.

programs.name: Social Services Block Grant (Title XX)
programs.federal_name: Social Security Title XX Social Services (HHS)
programs.about: State social service offices use this money to help families in a crisis, sometimes with basic items like a ramp or grab bars. It mostly serves people already on public aid.

programs.name: Georgia State Board of Workers' Compensation
programs.about: If a work injury makes it hard to live at home, Georgia workers' comp may pay for home changes. Ask your claims handler.

programs.name: Capital Gains Tax (cost basis)
programs.about: Money spent on accessibility can raise your home's cost basis, which may lower the taxable gain when you sell.

programs.name: Business Tax Deduction
programs.about: Owners who use property for business may be able to deduct accessibility work faster than other improvements.

programs.name: State/Local Sales Tax Exemption
programs.about: Some states or counties waive sales tax on ramp materials or lift equipment. Check with Georgia or your county tax office.

programs.name: Local Property Tax Exemption
programs.about: Home changes can raise a home's assessed value. Ask your local assessor whether accessibility work is exempt.

programs.name: Georgia Disabled Person Home Purchase or Retrofit Tax Credit
programs.about: A small Georgia income tax credit for a person with a permanent disability: up to $500 for buying a new home with set access features, or up to $125 for adding them to an existing home. You need a permanent disability parking permit, and unused credit carries forward 3 years.

notes: Georgia has a state tax credit for accessible home purchase or retrofit ($500 new home / $125 retrofit; requires a permanent disability parking permit). The aging division also lists in-home services that can include home repair.
